t: LeetCode 1492 — The kth Factor of n
o: We need the k-th smallest divisor of n, or -1 if fewer than k divisors exist. For n = 12, k = 3: divisors are [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12], so we return 3. For n = 7, k = 2: divisors are [1, 7], so we return 7. For n = 4, k = 4: only [1, 2, 4] exist, so we return -1. Since n <= 1000, even a linear scan works, but the follow-up asks for sublinear time, which factor-pair enumeration achieves.
k: Divisors come in pairs (i, n/i): scanning i up to sqrt(n) finds all of them in O(sqrt(n)) time.
Small factors (i <= sqrt(n)) appear first in ascending order; large factors (n/i) appear in descending order and must be reversed or counted from the end.
The total number of divisors is at most ~2*sqrt(n) candidates, so k can be checked against both halves.

a.i: Simply iterate i from 1 to n; every i with n % i == 0 is a divisor encountered in ascending order. Count them until reaching the k-th one. This is trivially correct because ascending iteration visits divisors in sorted order.
s: Loop i from 1 to n inclusive.
If n % i == 0, increment cnt; when cnt == k, return i immediately.
If the loop finishes without returning, return -1.
a.t: O(n) — single pass over all integers up to n.
a.sp: O(1) — only a counter is used.

a.i: Every divisor i <= sqrt(n) pairs with n/i >= sqrt(n). Scanning i from 1 to sqrt(n), small divisors arrive in ascending order; their complements n/i form the large half in descending order. So the full sorted list is: small divisors ascending, then large divisors reversed. We can count how many small divisors exist first, then decide whether the k-th factor lies in the small half or the large half without storing anything.
s: Let s = floor(sqrt(n)). First pass: count small divisors i <= s with n % i == 0; call this count c.
If k <= c, do a second scan of i from 1 upward counting divisors and return the k-th one.
Otherwise compute r = c - (k - c): the index (from the end) within the large half, since large divisors total c minus any perfect-square duplicate.
Second pass over i from s down to 1: whenever n % i == 0 and i != n/i, decrement r; when r == 0 return n/i.

c.python:
import math

class Solution:
    def kthFactor(self, n: int, k: int) -> int:
        s = int(math.isqrt(n))
        small = [i for i in range(1, s + 1) if n % i == 0]
        large = [n // i for i in range(s, 0, -1) if n % i == 0 and n // i != i]
        factors = small + large
        return factors[k - 1] if k <= len(factors) else -1

a.t: O(sqrt(n)) — one pass over i up to sqrt(n); building/merging lists is bounded by the same term.
a.sp: O(sqrt(n)) — stores at most 2*sqrt(n) divisors; can be reduced to O(1) with two counting passes.

w: In an interview, start with the brute force to establish correctness, then offer the sqrt decomposition as the follow-up answer — it demonstrates knowledge of divisor pairing. Key pitfalls: forgetting that perfect squares produce a duplicated middle divisor (i == n/i must be counted once), and misordering the large half (complements come out descending, so they must be reversed). Edge cases: n = 1 (only factor is 1), k larger than the divisor count, and prime n which has exactly two factors. Likely follow-ups: solve in O(1) space with two passes, or handle very large n where you would use prime factorization to enumerate divisors from the factorization instead.
